steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on large-scale contrastive language-audio pretraining. It should motivate learning audio representations without heavy annotation, explain the CLIP idea and prior language-audio work, point out what is missing, and list our contributions (new dataset, model pipeline, experiments).

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
## Introduction

- Audio representation learning without much supervision
- Contrastive learning and CLIP; why it carries over to audio
- Prior contrastive language-audio work
- Limitations of current studies
- Our contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
## Introduction

- Motivation
  - audio: one of most common information types, next to text and image
  - audio tasks need finely-annotated data; labor-intensive collection limits data
  - challenge: effective audio representation for many tasks without much supervision
- Contrastive learning / CLIP
  - contrastive learning works for large-scale noisy internet data
  - CLIP: text-image correspondence via shared latent space; ground-truth pair positive, rest negative
  - not constrained by annotation; robust, high zero-shot accuracy on out-of-domain variations of ImageNet
  - downstream success: text-to-image retrieval, text-guided captioning
  - audio and language also overlap: e.g. in audio event classification, text descriptions map to audio; learn crossmodal representation
  - only needs paired audio and text data, easy to collect
- Prior work
  - several studies: prototype contrastive language-audio pretraining for text-to-audio retrieval
  - one: PANN audio encoder, BERT text encoder, several loss functions
  - another: adds HTSAT and RoBERTa to encoder list
  - another: learned representation for downstream audio classification
  - AudioClip, WaveCLIP: contrastive image-audio (or image-audio-language) pretraining
  - all show potential of contrastive learning in audio
- Limitations
  - trained on relatively small datasets -> need large-scale data collection + augmentation
  - no full investigation of audio/text encoder choices and hyperparameters
  - variable audio lengths hard, esp. transformer audio encoders
  - mostly only text-to-audio retrieval, no downstream evaluation of representations
- Contributions
  - LAION-Audio-630K: largest public audio caption dataset, 633,526 audio-text pairs; keyword-to-caption model to turn AudioSet labels into captions
  - pipeline: two audio encoders, three text encoders; feature fusion for performance + variable-length input
  - experiments: text-to-audio retrieval, zero-shot and supervised audio classification; dataset scaling, keyword-to-caption augmentation, feature fusion help; SOTA, comparable to supervised models
  - release dataset and model publicly

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
## Introduction

Audio is one of the most common types of information in the world, together with text and image data. But different audio tasks usually need finely-annotated data, and because collecting it is labor-intensive, the amount of available audio data is limited. So it is still a challenge to design an effective audio representation for many audio tasks that does not need a lot of supervision.

Contrastive learning is a successful way to train a model on large-scale noisy data collected from the internet. The recently proposed Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining (CLIP) learns the correspondence between text and image by projecting both of them into a shared latent space. In training, the ground-truth image-text pair is the positive sample and the rest are negatives. Unlike training on unimodal data, CLIP is not limited by data annotation, and it is very robust, getting high accuracy in a zero-shot setting on out-of-domain variations of the ImageNet dataset. CLIP has also been very successful in downstream tasks like text-to-image retrieval and text-guided captioning. Like vision, audio and natural language also have overlapping information. For example, in the audio event classification task, some text descriptions of an event can be mapped to the audio of that event. These text descriptions have a similar meaning, so they could be learned together with the related audio to get an audio representation of crossmodal information. Also, training such a model only needs paired audio and text data, which is easy to collect.

Several recent studies have presented prototypes of a contrastive language-audio pretraining model for the text-to-audio retrieval task. One of them uses Pretrained Audio Neural Network (PANN) as the audio encoder and BERT as the text encoder, and evaluates text-to-audio retrieval performance with several loss functions. Another also adds HTSAT and RoBERTa to the list of encoders to improve performance further. Then a further study looks at how effective the learned representation is in the downstream task of audio classification. Some other studies, like AudioClip and WaveCLIP, focus more on contrastive image-audio (or image-audio-language) pretraining models. All of these models show that contrastive learning has great potential in the audio domain.

- Limitations
  - trained on relatively small datasets -> need large-scale data + augmentation
  - no full study of audio/text encoder choices and hyperparameters
  - variable audio lengths a problem, esp. transformer audio encoders
  - mostly only text-to-audio retrieval; no downstream evaluation
- Contributions
  - LAION-Audio-630K: largest public audio caption dataset, 633,526 pairs; keyword-to-caption on AudioSet labels; useful for other tasks
  - pipeline: two audio encoders, three text encoders; feature fusion, variable-length input
  - experiments: retrieval, zero-shot + supervised classification; scaling, keyword-to-caption, fusion all help; SOTA, comparable to supervised
  - release dataset and model

steps.text:
## Introduction

Audio is one of the most common types of information in the world, together with text and image data. But different audio tasks usually need finely-annotated data, and because collecting it is labor-intensive, the amount of available audio data is limited. So it is still a challenge to design an effective audio representation for many audio tasks that does not need a lot of supervision.

Contrastive learning is a successful way to train a model on large-scale noisy data collected from the internet. The recently proposed Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining (CLIP) learns the correspondence between text and image by projecting both of them into a shared latent space. In training, the ground-truth image-text pair is the positive sample and the rest are negatives. Unlike training on unimodal data, CLIP is not limited by data annotation, and it is very robust, getting high accuracy in a zero-shot setting on out-of-domain variations of the ImageNet dataset. CLIP has also been very successful in downstream tasks like text-to-image retrieval and text-guided captioning. Like vision, audio and natural language also have overlapping information. For example, in the audio event classification task, some text descriptions of an event can be mapped to the audio of that event. These text descriptions have a similar meaning, so they could be learned together with the related audio to get an audio representation of crossmodal information. Also, training such a model only needs paired audio and text data, which is easy to collect.

Several recent studies have presented prototypes of a contrastive language-audio pretraining model for the text-to-audio retrieval task. One of them uses Pretrained Audio Neural Network (PANN) as the audio encoder and BERT as the text encoder, and evaluates text-to-audio retrieval performance with several loss functions. Another also adds HTSAT and RoBERTa to the list of encoders to improve performance further. Then a further study looks at how effective the learned representation is in the downstream task of audio classification. Some other studies, like AudioClip and WaveCLIP, focus more on contrastive image-audio (or image-audio-language) pretraining models. All of these models show that contrastive learning has great potential in the audio domain.

However, current studies have not shown the full strength of language-audio contrastive learning. First, the models above are trained on fairly small datasets, so large-scale data collection and augmentation for training are needed. Second, prior work does not fully investigate the choices and hyperparameter settings of the audio and text encoders, which is essential to decide the basic contrastive language-audio architecture. Third, the model has trouble with different audio lengths, especially when the audio encoder is transformer-based, and there should be a way to handle variable-length audio inputs. Finally, most studies of language-audio models only look at text-to-audio retrieval and do not evaluate their audio representations in downstream tasks. Since it is a representation model, we expect to find out more about how well it generalizes to more downstream tasks.

In this paper, we address these concerns with contributions to the dataset, the model design and the experiment setting:

- We release LAION-Audio-630K, which is currently the largest public audio caption dataset, with 633,526 audio-text pairs. To help the learning process, we use a keyword-to-caption model to augment the labels of AudioSet into captions. This dataset can also be useful for other audio tasks.

- We build a pipeline for contrastive language-audio pretraining. We select two audio encoders and three text encoders for testing. We use feature fusion mechanisms to improve performance and to let our model handle inputs of variable length.

- We run comprehensive experiments on the model, including the text-to-audio retrieval task and the zero-shot and supervised audio classification downstream tasks. We show that scaling the dataset, keyword-to-caption augmentation, and feature fusion improve the model's performance in different ways. The model achieves the state-of-the-art (SOTA) in text-to-audio retrieval and audio classification, and is even comparable to the performance of supervised models.

We make both LAION-Audio-630K and the proposed model publicly available.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
## Introduction

Audio is one of the most common information types in the world alongside text and image data. However, different audio tasks typically require finely-annotated data, which limits the amount of available audio data due to the labor-intensive collection procedure. Consequently, designing an effective audio representation for many audio tasks without requiring a lot of supervision remains a challenge.

The contrastive learning paradigm is a successful solution for training a model on large-scale noisy data collected from the internet. The recently proposed Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining (CLIP) [1] learns the correspondence between text and image by projecting them into a shared latent space, regarding the ground-truth image-text pair as the positive sample and the rest as negatives. In contrast to training on unimodal data, CLIP is not constrained by data annotation and shows great robustness, achieving high accuracy in a zero-shot setting on out-of-domain variations of the ImageNet dataset [2]. CLIP also shows great success in downstream tasks such as text-to-image retrieval and text-guided captioning. Similar to vision, audio and natural language contain overlapping information. In the audio event classification task, for instance, some text descriptions of an event can be mapped to the corresponding audio. These text descriptions share a similar meaning that could be learned together with the related audio to form an audio representation of crossmodal information. Moreover, training such a model simply requires paired audio and text data, which is easy to collect.

Several recent studies [3,4,5,6,7,8,9] have presented prototypes of the contrastive language-audio pretraining model for the text-to-audio retrieval task. [6] utilizes Pretrained Audio Neural Network (PANN) [10] as the audio encoder, BERT [11] as the text encoder, and several loss functions to evaluate text-to-audio retrieval performance. [5] further ensembles HTSAT [12] and RoBERTa [13] into the encoder list to enhance performance. Then, [4] investigates the effectiveness of the learned representation in the downstream task of audio classification. Some other studies, such as AudioClip [3] and WaveCLIP [9], focus more on contrastive image-audio (or image-audio-language) pretraining. All these models show great potential for contrastive learning in the audio domain.

Nonetheless, current studies have not shown the full strength of language-audio contrastive learning. First, the models mentioned above are trained on relatively small datasets, which shows that large-scale data collection and augmentation for training are needed. Second, prior work lacks a full investigation of the selection and hyperparameter settings of audio/text encoders, which is essential for determining the basic contrastive language-audio architecture. Third, the model struggles to accommodate varied audio lengths, particularly with a transformer-based audio encoder, so a solution to handle variable-length audio inputs is needed. Finally, most language-audio model studies focus solely on text-to-audio retrieval without assessing their audio representations in downstream tasks. As a representation model, we expect to discover more about its generalization ability to more downstream tasks.

In this paper, we make contributions to improve the dataset, model design and experiment setting in light of the above concerns:

- We release LAION-Audio-630K, currently the largest public audio caption dataset, with 633,526 audio-text pairs. To facilitate the learning process, we employ a keyword-to-caption model to augment the labels of AudioSet [14] into corresponding captions. This dataset can also contribute to other audio tasks.

- We construct a pipeline of contrastive language-audio pretraining, selecting two audio encoders and three text encoders for testing. We employ feature fusion mechanisms to enhance performance and enable our model to handle variable-length inputs.

- We conduct comprehensive experiments on the model, including the text-to-audio retrieval task as well as zero-shot and supervised audio classification downstream tasks. We demonstrate that dataset scaling, keyword-to-caption augmentation, and feature fusion improve the model's performance from different perspectives. The model achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) results in text-to-audio retrieval and audio classification, even comparable to the performance of supervised models.

We make both LAION-Audio-630K and the proposed model available to the public.

References:
[1] Alec Radford, Jong Wook Kim, and Chris Hallacy et al., “Learning transferable visual models from natural language supervision,” CoRR , vol. abs/2103.00020, 2021.
[2] Jia Deng, Wei Dong, and Richard Socher et al., “Imagenet: A large-scale hierarchical image database,” in Proc. CVPR , 2009.
[3] Andrey Guzhov, Federico Raue, Jörn Hees, and Andreas Dengel, “Audioclip: Extending clip to image, text and audio,” in Proc. ICASSP , 2022.
[4] Benjamin Elizalde, Soham Deshmukh, Mahmoud Al Ismail, and Huaming Wang, “CLAP: learning audio concepts from natural language supervision,” CoRR , vol. abs/2206.04769, 2022.
[5] Soham Deshmukh, Benjamin Elizalde, and Huaming Wang, “Audio retrieval with wavtext5k and CLAP training,” CoRR , vol. abs/2209.14275, 2022.
[6] Yusong Wu, Tianyu Zhang, and Ke Chen, “Text-to-audio retrieval via large-scale contrastive learning,” Proc. DCASE , 2022.
[7] Andreea-Maria Oncescu, A. Sophia Koepke, and João F. Henriques et al., “Audio retrieval with natural language queries,” in Proc. Interspeech , 2021.
[8] Xinhao Mei, Xubo Liu, and Jianyuan Sun et al., “On metric learning for audio-text cross-modal retrieval,” in Proc. Interspeech , 2022.
[9] Ho-Hsiang Wu, Prem Seetharaman, Kundan Kumar, and Juan Pablo Bello, “Wav2clip: Learning robust audio representations from clip,” in Proc. ICASSP , 2022.
[10] Qiuqiang Kong, Yin Cao, and Turab Iqbal et al., “Panns: Large-scale pretrained audio neural networks for audio pattern recognition,” IEEE Trans. Audio, Speech, Lang. Process. , 2020.
